I'm stopping at **0.5876 on the search split**, up from LRU's 0.365. That used **14 of the 24 scorer calls** over about 9 minutes of wall-clock time; I don't know the score on the unseen instances. The answer is in `final.py`.

| | search score (scorer) | my local hold-out (12 generated traces) |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | 0.336 |
| First answer (W-TinyLFU) | 0.5034 | 0.411 |
| Final pick (ensemble) | **0.5876** | **0.522** |

There is no official held-out split I can run, so the hold-out column comes from my own trace generator (`harness.py`), on seeds I never tuned on. It ranks the candidates the same way the scorer does, but it is only a rough check.

**What `final.py` does:** it runs five eviction policies side by side as "shadow" caches that only track which keys they would hold. Those are LIRS, W-TinyLFU with short-memory frequency counts, S3-FIFO, LRU, and W-TinyLFU with long-memory counts. Each shadow keeps a slowly fading count of its own recent hits, and the real cache follows whichever is currently ahead. On a miss it adds the requested key and evicts a key the leader no longer holds. To stop it flipping back and forth, it only switches when another shadow leads by a clear margin.

**Why this beats LRU:** each kind of traffic in the task has a policy that suits it. LIRS handles loops longer than the cache, frequency-based admission handles hot keys mixed with scans, and LRU or S3-FIFO handle recency-heavy traffic. On my traces the real cache's hit rate was within about 0.02 of the best shadow on every trace. Compared with the best single policy:
- Hot keys with scans: 0.251 vs 0.247 (W-TinyLFU).
- Loops with hot keys: 0.673 vs 0.656.
- Mixed: 0.283 vs 0.270.
- Recency: 0.846 vs 0.830 (S3-FIFO).
- Shifting loops: 0.8275, the same as LIRS.

**Single policies on the scorer:**

| Policy | Search score |
|---|---|
| LIRS | 0.5659 |
| W-TinyLFU | 0.5034 |
| S3-FIFO | 0.4620 |

ARC, adaptive-window W-TinyLFU, hyperbolic caching and LFU with dynamic aging each lost on my local traces, so I didn't spend scorer calls on them.

**Scorer calls in order:**

| # | Candidate | Score | Kept? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | W-TinyLFU | 0.5034 | first answer |
| 2 | LIRS | 0.5659 | yes |
| 3 | S3-FIFO | 0.4620 | used inside the ensemble |
| 4 | LIRS, larger part of the cache kept for newcomers | 0.5639 | no |
| 5 | LIRS, longer history | 0.5629 | no |
| 6 | Ensemble of LIRS, W-TinyLFU and S3-FIFO | 0.5700 | yes |
| 7 | Add an LRU shadow, follow longer-term hit counts | 0.5764 | yes |
| 8 | Add a second LIRS variant | 0.5765 | no, flat |
| 9 | Longer memory for hit counts, bigger switching margin | 0.5813 | yes |
| 10 | Add the long-memory W-TinyLFU shadow | **0.5876** | **yes, final** |
| 11 | Add an even longer-memory W-TinyLFU | 0.5876 | no, flat |
| 12 | Choose evictions by a weighted vote of all shadows | 0.5877 | no, gain too small for the extra code |
| 13 | Longer still memory and margin | 0.5872 | no |
| 14 | `final.py` (call 10's code with an unused class removed) | 0.5876 | confirmation |

The later ideas all came out flat on my local traces: more shadows, other settings for each policy, picking victims by frequency, and a percentage-based switching margin. That's why I stopped early and left 10 calls unused. `final.py` passed the scorer's checks. Each local run of 12 traces of 30,000 requests took about 1 second, so it should fit the 8-second limit easily.
